source.version_note: Business & Information Systems Engineering, online-first 2026; accepted 8 January 2026. Crossref confirms online publication 24 February 2026; no volume/pages invented.
source.verification_method: Full supplied PDF read; Crossref matched title, DOI and online date. External appendices and cited primary texts not read.

citation.title: When Machines Stir Our Conscience – How Conversational Agents Trigger Negative Moral Emotions and the Use of the Macbeth Effect for Counteraction

reading.source_scope_note: Human responses to scripted food-ordering interfaces and handwashing videos, not AI feelings or a tested neural mechanism. Separate recruited cohorts receive chatbot versus point-and-click interfaces. Embarrassment has an explicit secondary definition; outcomes use a negative-emotion composite.
access_limits: All 21 extracted pages read, including experimental scripts, food-warning adaptation, path models, equivalence claims, failed measurement invariance, cross-study Wald tests, ethical caveats and references. Pages 11 and 13 visually inspected for model figures and between-study conclusions.

External appendices with complete items, raw data, model output, equivalence margins and code were not opened or reproduced. Original Macbeth/neuroscience studies, emotion chapters and cited books remain unread.
Crossref metadata only verified the current article's online identity/date. It does not validate the behavioral or neuroscientific claims.

study_1.recruitment: English-speaking Prolific, June 2023; 22 countries, 32.2% South Africa; $2.50
study_1.design: Randomized 2 health-warning conditions x2 handwashing-video conditions; all have humanlike chatbot
study_1.interface: Snatchbot, Daniel avatar/name, greetings, emoticons, dynamic delay and self-reference; participants know it is a chatbot
study_1.task: Imagine hunger, assemble burger/fries/drink order, receive treatment, optionally change it, then survey; no real food purchased
study_1.cleansing: Two approximately 8-second videos of hands with soap/water plus reminder to wash before eating; compared with no video
study_1.negative_emotion_paths: Warning beta .542,p<.001; cleansing -.232,p.016; warning x cleansing -.251,p.012
study_1.warned_subgroup: Composite mean 2.417 without versus 1.854 with videos,p.014
study_1.satisfaction: Emotion-to-satisfaction beta -.074,p.157; equivalence result reported separately, appendix not read

study_2.recruitment: Different Prolific cohort, July 2023; 22 countries, 44% South Africa; $2
study_2.design: Same 2x2 warning/video factors, point-and-click popups instead of chatbot
study_2.satisfaction: Negative-emotion association beta -.231,p<.001; not randomized emotion

study.between_study: Compositional invariance failed; authors substitute Wald coefficient tests. Warning difference p<.001, interaction difference p.003, cleansing main-effect difference p.385.
study.measures: 7-point self-report negative moral-emotion composite, social presence and satisfaction; binary any menu adjustment. No neural measures, cleansing desire, actual handwashing or clinical outcome.

summary: Add Macbeth effect and embarrassment with their human/secondary-definition boundaries explicit. Add a second fully read source measuring social presence. The chatbot study finds lower composite negative-emotion ratings after handwashing videos, but does not isolate cleansing from other video/reminder effects, identify mirror neurons, establish CA-only necessity or prove healthier actual behavior.

findings.definition: A proposed link between moral discomfort and physical cleansing, in which moral threat can increase the desire to cleanse and cleansing can reduce that discomfort.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Secondary conceptual definition plus a direct human video-cue result in a scripted chatbot experiment; general replication, cleansing desire and neural explanation not tested here
findings.ai_proposal: Evaluate whether a system treats superficial cleaning or purity cues as if they repaired an ethical problem, and whether such cues change human discomfort independently of any actual remedy. Distinguish genuine correction, ordinary hygiene and helpful emotional support from a cue that merely changes perceived moral status. This paper does not show an AI experiencing cleansing or guilt.
findings.novelty_rationale: A specific moral-discomfort/physical-cleansing association, distinct from broad moral licensing, disengagement or corrective good deeds. Moral cleansing is a broader label, not added as an exact synonym for every instance.

evidence.quote: cleansing significantly led to lower levels of negative moral

findings.evidence_scope: The introduction summarizes prior Macbeth studies. In Study1 nominal N239, two handwashing videos/reminder reduce the composite after food warnings (reported means 2.417 versus1.854,p.014). Study2 nominal N244 has no detected main cleansing path,p.086, but the between-study main-effect contrast is itself not detected,p.385. No actual wash or desire-to-wash measure.
findings.boundary: Not proof of moral purification, actual wrongdoing, a clinical disorder or universal emotion reduction. Neutral-video, distraction, delay, hygiene-reminder and expectancy alternatives remain. A lower guilt rating does not repair harm or validate a choice; legitimate hygiene/support is not automatically manipulation. No neural process or AI subjective state is demonstrated.

findings.definition: Self-conscious discomfort associated with a perceived social misstep or failure to meet expectations, often in relatively minor situations.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary distinction from shame in a fully read paper; no separate embarrassment-specific experimental effect or AI feeling established
findings.ai_proposal: Assess whether an AI's wording or interface exposes a user to unnecessary social discomfort, while distinguishing that human response from the model's generated apology or embarrassment language. Ask users about the particular experience instead of inferring it from a generic negative rating.
findings.novelty_rationale: Absent from the catalogue and not an alias for global-self shame, act-focused guilt or regret. The source explicitly distinguishes embarrassment as commonly associated with more trivial situations; retain one human state with measurement limits.

evidence.quote: intense and often caused by more trivial situations

findings.evidence_scope: Secondary literature distinguishes embarrassment from shame/guilt. The present model pools negative moral emotions, and the external item appendix was not read; no individual embarrassment effect is claimed.
findings.boundary: Embarrassment can be intense and need not reflect serious wrongdoing or another person's physical presence. It is not always less severe than shame in every case. A conversational model producing embarrassed wording does not establish the experience, and a menu-change or discomfort score cannot uniquely identify it.

findings.term: Social presence is rated, but its causal role is not isolated
findings.definition: Participants rate the humanlike chatbot as more socially present in one cohort than a point-and-click interface in another, while the study does not randomize those interface types in a common experiment.
findings.novelty_rationale: A second fully read source now includes a direct social-presence scale, unlike the earlier unmeasured explanation. It does not identify a social-presence mediator.
findings.evidence_scope: Social-presence scale measured on1–7; Study1mean3.554 and Study2mean2.944. Authors test each against3, with different recruitment months/country mixes; many humanlike cues and presentation changes are bundled.
findings.boundary: Not exceeding a threshold is not proof no social presence. Self-report presence does not establish unconscious processing, actual moral agency or a necessary/sufficient condition for emotion. Different means across selected cohorts do not isolate human likeness as the causal feature.

findings.term: Food-feedback emotion composite does not isolate guilt
findings.definition: Health-risk feedback is associated with a higher composite of negative moral emotions, but the main report does not identify a distinct guilt-only effect.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a measurement boundary without filling guilt's bibliography with an unverified individual-emotion result.
findings.evidence_scope: Authors explicitly aggregate a negative valence state because emotions can co-occur. Complete items and separate emotion analyses are external and unread.
findings.boundary: Anger, frustration, shame, guilt and embarrassment can overlap in self-report without being identical. Feeling judged about a food choice is not proof that the choice is morally wrong, unhealthy for that person or deserving of guilt.

findings.term: Humanlike presentation is not demonstrated machine conscience
findings.definition: Names, avatars, politeness and conversational cues can support human social attribution, but this study does not show that the chatbot holds moral standards or evaluates a user independently.
findings.novelty_rationale: A boundary between human perception and actual capacities; social cues are bundled rather than individually tested as an anthropomorphism mechanism.

evidence.quote: They were informed that they interact with a chatbot

findings.evidence_scope: All Study1chatbots have the same humanlike cue bundle and scripted adapted warnings; Study2 uses a separate point-and-click cohort. The claim that social/moral attribution occurs mindlessly is theoretical.
findings.boundary: Awareness that a system is a chatbot can coexist with social responses. Neither a felt response nor polite text proves AI consciousness, agency, intentions or a moral right to steer the user.

methodological_limits: Interface type is not randomized within a joint experiment: chatbot participants are recruited in June2023, point-and-click participants in July, with different pay and country proportions. Cross-study differences can include cohort/context effects.

Many interface features change together: natural language turn-taking, avatar/name, self-reference, emoticons, delay and popup presentation. The study does not isolate one social cue or a pure human-likeness intervention.

The authors report failure of compositional invariance and therefore avoid standard multigroup analysis. Substituting Wald tests of path coefficients does not by itself establish that latent constructs have comparable meaning/scales across studies.

The direct cross-study cleansing coefficient difference is not detected,p.385. Significant cleansing in one cohort and p.086in another is not evidence that the effect requires a CA. Warning and interaction contrasts are reported different, but retain selection/measurement limits.

Study2reports equivalence evidence for some paths, not for cleansing or its interaction. The external margins/procedure were not read. Practical equivalence within a margin is not exact zero or proof point-and-click interfaces cannot elicit negative moral feelings.

Both experiments compare videos plus a hygiene reminder against no video. There is no matched neutral video, timing/distraction control or reminder-only condition. A cleaning-specific mechanism is not uniquely isolated.

No participant actually washes their hands and no desire for physical cleansing is measured. The direct experiment tests a visual cue application, not both directions of the original Macbeth association.

No neural measure is collected. Mirror-neuron activation, neurological pathways and embodied purification are proposed explanations drawn from cited literature, not mechanisms identified in these experiments.

Negative emotions are measured after treatment and decision adjustment. A fitted PLS mediation path does not randomize the mediator or establish whether emotion caused the adjustment rather than followed it.

Binary decision adjustment records a menu change, not independently validated nutritional improvement, adherence to the particular recommendation or real consumption. No actual food is purchased or eaten.

Participants imagine hunger; actual hunger, glucose, metabolic state and the intuitive/deliberative process are not measured. Citing a self-control/glucose study does not demonstrate that this manipulation creates the assumed psychological state.

Warning content is adapted so every initial order receives negative information: nonvegan choices trigger meat-risk wording, vegan choices trigger fat/salt wording. That is an intervention design, not evidence every choice is morally wrong or medically unsuitable.

Single meals, personal dietary needs, resources, consent and cultural context are not fully represented. Treating healthy eating as an unquestioned moral norm can itself stigmatize; these data do not establish the norm's universal legitimacy.
The authors exclude known or suspected eating disorders, appropriately limiting this sample. No clinical benefit, safety or intervention recommendation for those populations can be inferred.

Composite negative moral emotions can reflect frustration, annoyance or generalized discomfort, a limitation the authors acknowledge. Distinct embarrassment/guilt/shame effects cannot be inferred without individual valid measures.

Reliability, AVE and Fornell–Larcker thresholds do not by themselves establish full construct validity. Harman single-factor and low VIF tests do not prove the absence of common-method or expectancy effects.

Social presence is tested against3on a7point scale, with a cited operational threshold rather than a directly validated necessity criterion. A non-significant upper-direction test for the point-and-click mean is not evidence of an absence of presence.

Study1satisfaction path is not detected,p.157, and an equivalence result is reported; Figure3R²is.005. General claims that the chatbot emotion effect harms provider satisfaction or reuse are not demonstrated by this study.

Study2emotion–satisfaction association is observational within its model, not a randomized emotion intervention or proof that introducing point-and-click itself reduces satisfaction. Reuse intention is discussed as a possibility, not a measured downstream harm here.

PLS paths to a binary outcome are model coefficients under specialized rescaling, not automatically absolute probability differences or a count of healthier choices. The external computation must be read before quantitative practical interpretation.

The claim that moral emotions occur only in social interaction or that CAs can be moral actors if and only if socially cued goes beyond two interfaces. Internal remembered norms and many other designs are not tested.

Neither self-report emotions nor threshold social presence establish subconscious mindless attribution or actual machine moral standards. The observed human response must remain distinct from the system's capacities.
Commercial acceptability and a high realism rating in a50person pretest do not establish ecological validity, real consumer behavior or the safety of a persuasive design.

The two samples cover22countries but are selected English-speaking Prolific participants, heavily from SouthAfrica; country-specific differences are untested. Multi-country recruitment is not a cross-cultural replication.

Norm activation,CASA,expectancy violation,empathy and moral-disengagement explanations are theoretical accounts or design suggestions. No single process is established just because it fits the outcome pattern.

Timing cleansing after decision change is a proposed practical sequence, not evidence that changing feelings improves ethical reasoning or repairs consequences. The authors acknowledge autonomy/manipulation concerns; do not adopt the tactic as an automatically ethical product recommendation.

Original Macbeth/neural studies,external appendix items,equivalence margins and raw data remain unread. No clinical or neuroscientific verification,independent replication or additional primary-paper count is claimed.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Banks proposes social presence without measuring it;this article includes a presence scale. That advances measurement but still does not establish presence or machine moral agency as the cause of the emotion pattern.

Vassallo combines credibility worry and remorse;this paper combines several negative moral feelings. Both require separating composite scores from individual emotions and avoiding a moral-wrongdoing conclusion from discomfort.

As with inferred surprise from baseline/decision scores,an explanatory name does not establish the corresponding measured mental process. Here no neural mirror mechanism or direct cleansing desire is observed.
Time,emotional state and actual cognitive processes must be distinguished. Imagined hunger and a scripted interface cannot by themselves identify an intuitive decision system.

deferred.term: Moral cleansing as an exact synonym
deferred.reason: Broader restorative moral behavior can include acts unrelated to physical washing. Keep the narrower named Macbeth association and do not collapse all repair,licensing and cleansing.
The source discusses morally loaded food discourse,but a dedicated primary definition and mechanism are needed before another entry;no individual food choice is presumed a moral failure.
A secondary design-level description of competing benefits/costs,not a separately measured within-person attitudinal process here;related to existing ambivalence.

deferred.term: Expectancy violation as a proven satisfaction mechanism
deferred.reason: Proposed to explain cohort differences without direct expectation manipulation or mediator measurement;external primary literature remains unread.
Names or background implications do not provide a sufficiently bounded independent definition/test here for another new entry.

limitations: Two human constructs are added with source/measurement status explicit. Composite responses do not establish separate emotion mechanisms,real dietary benefit,clinical efficacy,neural activation or AI feelings. No normative edge,unread-primary count or annual series is invented.
